title: Hormonal Regulation of Homeostasis
purpose: Codex-ready authored formative bank. Source quizzes and textbook review were used for scope/difficulty calibration; these are fresh practice items rather than a learner-facing answer-key dump.

lessons.label: Hormones, target cells and mechanisms of action
Integrated chapter review and final check

concepts.definition: the nervous system typically sends rapid, targeted electrochemical signals through neurons; the endocrine system sends hormones through blood and often produces slower, longer-lasting, broader responses
concepts.scenario: A reflex withdraws a hand within moments, while a hormonal change may influence metabolism for much longer.
concepts.misconception: The nervous and endocrine systems operate independently and never share messengers or feedback control.
concepts.cue: Compare route, speed, duration and target range.
concepts.explanation: The systems are distinct but closely integrated in homeostatic regulation.

concepts.definition: a ductless gland that releases hormones into extracellular fluid and then the bloodstream
concepts.scenario: Pancreatic endocrine cells release insulin into nearby capillaries.
concepts.misconception: Endocrine glands deliver hormones through ducts directly to target organs.
concepts.cue: Endocrine means secretion into blood, not through a duct.
concepts.explanation: Hormones circulate widely but only receptor-bearing target cells respond appropriately.

concepts.definition: a target cell responds to a hormone because it has a compatible receptor protein
concepts.scenario: hGH circulates widely but only cells with appropriate receptors respond directly.
concepts.misconception: Every cell exposed to a circulating hormone must respond in the same way.
concepts.cue: Circulation is broad; receptor expression gives specificity.
concepts.explanation: Hormone concentration alone does not determine which cells respond.

concepts.definition: water-soluble hormones usually bind membrane receptors and trigger intracellular cascades; lipid-soluble steroid hormones can cross the membrane and bind intracellular receptors
concepts.scenario: Epinephrine binds a surface receptor, while cortisol can enter a target cell and act through an intracellular receptor.
concepts.misconception: All hormones enter the nucleus directly because they travel in blood.
concepts.cue: Ask whether the messenger can cross the lipid bilayer.
concepts.explanation: Solubility influences receptor location and signalling mechanism.
sourceRefs: Teacher slides: Two types of hormones

concepts.definition: a response reduces or counteracts the original change, tending to return a regulated variable toward its normal range
concepts.scenario: Rising thyroxine feeds back to reduce further TSH drive.
concepts.misconception: Negative feedback means the response is harmful or undesirable.
concepts.cue: Negative means opposing the deviation, not 'bad'.
concepts.explanation: Most endocrine homeostatic loops use negative feedback.

concepts.definition: a response amplifies the initiating change until an external endpoint stops the loop
concepts.scenario: Oxytocin-driven uterine contractions increase cervical stimulation, which promotes more oxytocin release during labour.
concepts.misconception: Positive feedback is the usual mechanism for keeping variables close to a set range.
concepts.cue: Positive feedback reinforces rather than reverses the initial change.
concepts.explanation: It is useful for processes that need to run to completion, such as childbirth.
sourceRefs: Teacher slides: Positive vs negative feedback

concepts.definition: the hypothalamus regulates the anterior pituitary through releasing/inhibiting hormones and the posterior pituitary through neurosecretory axons
concepts.scenario: A hypothalamic releasing hormone travels through a portal system and changes anterior-pituitary secretion.
concepts.misconception: The anterior and posterior pituitary are regulated in exactly the same way.
concepts.cue: Anterior uses portal blood; posterior stores/releases hypothalamic hormones from axon terminals.
concepts.explanation: The two lobes have different relationships with the hypothalamus.

concepts.definition: neural tissue that stores and releases ADH and oxytocin synthesized by hypothalamic neurosecretory cells
concepts.scenario: ADH is made in the hypothalamus, transported down axons, then released from posterior-pituitary terminals into blood.
concepts.misconception: The posterior pituitary synthesizes ADH and oxytocin.
concepts.cue: Distinguish produced from stored/released.
concepts.explanation: This produced-versus-released distinction is essential.

concepts.definition: endocrine tissue that synthesizes and releases hormones such as hGH, TSH, ACTH, PRL, FSH and LH under hypothalamic control
concepts.scenario: TSH is synthesized by anterior-pituitary cells and released when hypothalamic/pituitary control signals favour secretion.
concepts.misconception: All pituitary hormones are made in the hypothalamus.
concepts.cue: Anterior pituitary is a true hormone-synthesizing endocrine gland.
concepts.explanation: Its hormones include both direct-acting and tropic hormones.

concepts.definition: a hormone whose major target is another endocrine gland, stimulating that gland to release another hormone
concepts.scenario: TSH acts on the thyroid; ACTH acts on the adrenal cortex.
concepts.misconception: Every hormone released by the pituitary is tropic.
concepts.cue: The target is another endocrine gland.
concepts.explanation: TSH and ACTH are clear examples; not every pituitary hormone fits this definition.

concepts.definition: an anterior-pituitary hormone that promotes growth and metabolism directly and through liver-derived growth factors
concepts.scenario: During childhood, excessive hGH can cause extreme linear growth; deficiency can cause proportionate short stature.
concepts.misconception: hGH acts only on bone and has no metabolic effects.
concepts.cue: Think growth plus metabolism, with an important liver growth-factor pathway.
concepts.explanation: Timing matters: excess before growth plates close differs from excess in adults.

concepts.definition: excess hGH before growth plates close causes excessive height; excess after skeletal growth produces tissue/bone thickening rather than major height increase
concepts.scenario: An adult develops enlarged hands, feet and facial bones from chronic excess hGH.
concepts.misconception: Excess hGH causes the same growth pattern at every age.
concepts.cue: Ask whether long-bone growth plates are still capable of lengthening.
concepts.explanation: The developmental stage changes the phenotype of hGH excess.

concepts.definition: a hypothalamic hormone released from the posterior pituitary that increases kidney water reabsorption when body fluids are too concentrated or volume/pressure is low
concepts.scenario: Dehydration increases ADH release, producing lower-volume, more concentrated urine.
concepts.misconception: ADH is synthesized by the posterior pituitary and makes the kidneys excrete more water.
concepts.cue: Anti-diuretic means reducing water loss in urine.
concepts.explanation: ADH is produced in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary.

concepts.definition: a disorder involving inadequate ADH production/release or response, causing excessive dilute urine and dehydration risk
concepts.scenario: A person produces very large volumes of dilute urine despite needing to conserve water.
concepts.misconception: Diabetes insipidus is caused by insulin deficiency and high blood glucose.
concepts.cue: This condition is about water balance/ADH, not glucose/insulin.
concepts.explanation: It is distinct from diabetes mellitus despite sharing part of the name.

concepts.definition: a thyroid hormone that increases metabolic activity and supports growth/development; its production depends on iodine
concepts.scenario: Low T4 reduces negative feedback and can allow TSH to remain elevated.
concepts.misconception: Thyroxine acts only on one small target organ.
concepts.cue: Connect TSH, thyroid, metabolism and negative feedback.
concepts.explanation: T4 has broad systemic metabolic effects.

concepts.definition: too little thyroid hormone generally slows metabolic processes; excess thyroid hormone generally accelerates them
concepts.scenario: Fatigue, cold intolerance and weight gain are consistent with low thyroid activity; heat intolerance and weight loss are consistent with high activity.
concepts.misconception: Hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism produce the same metabolic symptoms.
concepts.cue: Low T4 slows; high T4 speeds metabolic activity.
concepts.explanation: Symptoms reflect changes in metabolic rate, though real diagnosis requires clinical assessment.
sourceRefs: Teacher slides: Problems with Thyroxine Production

concepts.definition: insufficient iodine can reduce thyroid-hormone synthesis; reduced feedback allows persistent TSH stimulation, enlarging the thyroid
concepts.scenario: Low dietary iodine is followed by low T4 and chronically high TSH drive.
concepts.misconception: A goitre from iodine deficiency occurs because TSH is too low to stimulate the thyroid.
concepts.cue: Trace the feedback consequence of low T4.
concepts.explanation: The enlargement reflects prolonged stimulation by TSH.

concepts.definition: PTH raises blood calcium by promoting bone calcium release, kidney reabsorption and vitamin-D-supported intestinal absorption; calcitonin can lower blood calcium, though its adult human role is comparatively minor
concepts.scenario: Falling blood Ca2+ increases PTH secretion from parathyroid glands.
concepts.misconception: PTH lowers blood calcium by driving calcium into bone.
concepts.cue: PTH pushes blood calcium up.
concepts.explanation: PTH is the major regulator emphasized for low blood calcium; calcitonin opposes high calcium but is less dominant in adult humans.

concepts.definition: the inner adrenal medulla produces epinephrine/norepinephrine for rapid stress responses; the outer cortex produces steroid hormones including cortisol and aldosterone
concepts.scenario: A sympathetic nerve signal directly stimulates the adrenal medulla during acute stress.
concepts.misconception: The adrenal cortex and medulla release the same hormones through the same control pathway.
concepts.cue: Inner = medulla = fast catecholamine response; outer = cortex = steroid hormones.
concepts.explanation: Anatomy maps directly onto hormone type and control pathway.

concepts.definition: adrenal-medulla hormones released rapidly under sympathetic nervous-system control that support fight-or-flight physiology
concepts.scenario: Heart rate, breathing, blood pressure and blood glucose rise rapidly during an acute threat.
concepts.misconception: ACTH must first travel through blood before the adrenal medulla can release epinephrine.
concepts.cue: The medulla is under direct nervous control in this pathway.
concepts.explanation: This explains why the short-term response begins quickly.

concepts.definition: a glucocorticoid from the adrenal cortex that supports longer-term stress by increasing energy availability and suppressing inflammatory/immune activity
concepts.scenario: ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex, increasing cortisol; high cortisol feeds back to hypothalamic/pituitary control.
concepts.misconception: Cortisol increases inflammation as a major long-term stress effect.
concepts.cue: Textbook: cortisol is anti-inflammatory, not pro-inflammatory.
concepts.explanation: Cortisol mobilizes fuel and suppresses inflammatory/immune responses; chronic excess can be harmful.

concepts.definition: hypothalamic signal → anterior pituitary ACTH → adrenal cortex cortisol, with cortisol negative feedback
concepts.scenario: A sustained stressor recruits a slower hormone cascade than direct sympathetic stimulation of the adrenal medulla.
concepts.misconception: The adrenal medulla and cortex are activated by identical upstream signals.
concepts.cue: Think hormone cascade rather than direct sympathetic nerve stimulation.
concepts.explanation: This pathway supports the longer-lasting stress response.

concepts.definition: a mineralocorticoid from the adrenal cortex that increases renal sodium reabsorption, promoting water retention and increased blood volume/pressure
concepts.scenario: More sodium is retained by distal nephron regions, and water follows osmotically.
concepts.misconception: Aldosterone lowers blood pressure by increasing sodium loss in urine.
concepts.cue: Retain sodium, then retain water.
concepts.explanation: For this course, focus on adrenal-cortex source and kidney effect; do not teach ACTH as the sole/primary physiological regulator of aldosterone.

concepts.definition: a pancreatic beta-cell hormone released when blood glucose is high; it promotes glucose uptake/use and glycogen formation, lowering blood glucose
concepts.scenario: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, rising blood glucose stimulates insulin secretion.
concepts.misconception: Insulin raises blood glucose by breaking liver glycogen into glucose.
concepts.cue: Insulin moves the regulated variable down after a meal.
concepts.explanation: Insulin and glucagon act antagonistically in glucose homeostasis.
sourceRefs: Teacher slides: Hormones of the Pancreas

concepts.definition: a pancreatic alpha-cell hormone released when blood glucose is low; it promotes liver glucose release, including glycogen breakdown, raising blood glucose
concepts.scenario: Between meals, falling blood glucose stimulates glucagon secretion.
concepts.misconception: Glucagon is released from beta cells after a meal to lower blood glucose.
concepts.cue: Glucagon moves blood glucose up.
concepts.explanation: Its action complements insulin in a negative-feedback system.
sourceRefs: Teacher slides: Hormones of the Pancreas

concepts.definition: a disorder of insulin production or response that causes chronic difficulty regulating blood glucose
concepts.scenario: Type 1 involves autoimmune destruction of beta cells; type 2 commonly involves insulin resistance and can progress to impaired insulin production.
concepts.misconception: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus have the same immediate underlying cause.
concepts.cue: Type 1: beta-cell destruction; Type 2: insulin resistance is central.
concepts.explanation: Both can produce hyperglycemia, but their pathophysiology differs.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which statement best describes an endocrine gland?
choices: It secretes hormones into the bloodstream without a duct
It carries electrical impulses down an axon
It releases digestive enzymes only through ducts
It must be located in the brain
authoredQuestions.answer: It secretes hormones into the bloodstream without a duct
authoredQuestions.explanation: Endocrine secretion enters extracellular fluid/blood for circulation.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Why are many endocrine responses slower than nervous responses?
choices: Hormones must be released and transported through blood to target cells
Hormones cannot bind receptors
Endocrine glands have no blood supply
Nervous signals always travel through hormones
authoredQuestions.answer: Hormones must be released and transported through blood to target cells
authoredQuestions.explanation: Neural signals are carried rapidly along specialized cells; endocrine messages rely on secretion and circulation.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Why does a circulating hormone affect some cells more than others?
choices: Only target cells have the appropriate receptor and signalling machinery
Only target cells receive blood
Hormones never leave one organ
Target cells are always neurons
authoredQuestions.answer: Only target cells have the appropriate receptor and signalling machinery
authoredQuestions.explanation: Wide circulation does not mean universal response.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which pairing is most consistent with hormone solubility?
choices: Cortisol — intracellular receptor
Epinephrine — intracellular steroid receptor only
Insulin — freely diffuses through membrane to nuclear receptor
hGH — crosses the lipid bilayer without a receptor
authoredQuestions.answer: Cortisol — intracellular receptor
authoredQuestions.explanation: Lipid-soluble steroid hormones can cross membranes and bind intracellular receptors.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which change is an example of negative feedback?
choices: Rising T4 suppresses further TSH drive
Cervical stretch increases oxytocin release during labour
A response amplifies the initial stimulus until birth
A hormone makes its own release increase indefinitely
authoredQuestions.answer: Rising T4 suppresses further TSH drive
authoredQuestions.cue: Negative feedback opposes the deviation or further output.
authoredQuestions.explanation: Thyroxine feedback limits upstream stimulation.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which feature distinguishes positive feedback from negative feedback?
choices: Positive feedback reinforces the initiating change
Positive feedback always restores a variable toward its set range
Positive feedback is always harmful
Positive feedback cannot involve hormones
authoredQuestions.answer: Positive feedback reinforces the initiating change
authoredQuestions.explanation: The loop usually ends at an external endpoint rather than by self-correction.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which statement about the posterior pituitary is correct?
choices: It stores and releases ADH and oxytocin made in the hypothalamus
It synthesizes TSH and ACTH
It produces insulin
It is the main source of thyroxine
authoredQuestions.answer: It stores and releases ADH and oxytocin made in the hypothalamus
authoredQuestions.explanation: Hypothalamic neurons synthesize these hormones; posterior-pituitary terminals release them.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which pair contains two anterior-pituitary tropic hormones?
choices: TSH and ACTH
ADH and oxytocin
Insulin and glucagon
Cortisol and aldosterone
authoredQuestions.answer: TSH and ACTH
authoredQuestions.explanation: TSH targets thyroid; ACTH targets adrenal cortex.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Why does excess hGH in adulthood produce acromegaly rather than extreme height?
choices: Long-bone growth plates have largely closed, so tissues thicken rather than lengthen greatly
Adults no longer have hGH receptors
The posterior pituitary destroys hGH
Adult hGH only affects the pancreas
authoredQuestions.answer: Long-bone growth plates have largely closed, so tissues thicken rather than lengthen greatly
authoredQuestions.cue: Timing relative to skeletal growth matters.
authoredQuestions.explanation: The same hormone excess has different effects before and after longitudinal growth ends.

authoredQuestions.prompt: What happens when ADH levels rise during dehydration?
choices: Kidney water reabsorption increases and urine volume decreases
Kidney water reabsorption decreases and urine volume increases
Blood becomes more concentrated because more water is lost
The pancreas releases glucagon to remove water
authoredQuestions.answer: Kidney water reabsorption increases and urine volume decreases
authoredQuestions.explanation: ADH helps conserve body water.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes diabetes insipidus from diabetes mellitus?
choices: Diabetes insipidus is primarily an ADH/water-balance problem; diabetes mellitus is an insulin/glucose-regulation problem
Both are caused only by lack of insulin
Both are caused only by excess ADH
Diabetes mellitus is a disorder of semicircular canals
authoredQuestions.answer: Diabetes insipidus is primarily an ADH/water-balance problem; diabetes mellitus is an insulin/glucose-regulation problem
authoredQuestions.cue: The shared name does not mean the same hormone system.
authoredQuestions.explanation: The two conditions involve different regulated variables and hormones.

authoredQuestions.prompt: A patient has a poorly functioning thyroid and low T4. If the hypothalamus and pituitary are functioning, what pattern is most expected?
choices: Low T4 and elevated TSH drive
High T4 and low TSH
High T4 and high insulin
Low T4 and no possible change in TSH
authoredQuestions.answer: Low T4 and elevated TSH drive
authoredQuestions.cue: Reduced negative feedback allows more upstream stimulation.
authoredQuestions.explanation: The pituitary continues trying to stimulate the underactive thyroid.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Why can iodine deficiency produce a goitre?
choices: Low thyroid-hormone synthesis weakens negative feedback, so persistent TSH stimulation enlarges the thyroid
Iodine directly blocks TSH receptors
High T4 permanently shuts off the thyroid
Iodine is needed to make insulin
authoredQuestions.answer: Low thyroid-hormone synthesis weakens negative feedback, so persistent TSH stimulation enlarges the thyroid
authoredQuestions.explanation: The enlargement is a consequence of chronic stimulation when hormone synthesis remains limited.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which hormone is released when blood calcium falls and acts to raise it?
choices: PTH
Calcitonin
Insulin
ADH
authoredQuestions.answer: PTH
authoredQuestions.cue: Parathyroid hormone pushes blood Ca2+ upward.
authoredQuestions.explanation: PTH acts on bone, kidney, and indirectly intestinal calcium absorption.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which statement about calcitonin is most accurate for this course?
choices: It can lower blood calcium, but its regulatory role in adult humans is relatively minor compared with PTH
It is the main hormone that raises blood calcium
It is secreted from the parathyroid when calcium is low
It directly triggers fight-or-flight
authoredQuestions.answer: It can lower blood calcium, but its regulatory role in adult humans is relatively minor compared with PTH
authoredQuestions.cue: The textbook explicitly qualifies its role in humans.
authoredQuestions.explanation: Do not present calcitonin and PTH as perfectly equal regulators in adult humans.

authoredQuestions.prompt: What directly stimulates the adrenal medulla during an acute stress response?
choices: Sympathetic neurons
TSH
Insulin
PTH
authoredQuestions.answer: Sympathetic neurons
authoredQuestions.explanation: The medulla is stimulated neurally, enabling fast catecholamine release.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which response is most consistent with epinephrine during fight-or-flight?
choices: Increased heart rate, breathing and blood glucose
Reduced heart rate and increased digestion
Lower blood pressure and lower glucose
Increased urine water loss as the primary response
authoredQuestions.answer: Increased heart rate, breathing and blood glucose
authoredQuestions.cue: Prepare the body for immediate action.
authoredQuestions.explanation: Catecholamines coordinate rapid cardiovascular, respiratory and metabolic changes.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which sequence correctly traces cortisol release?
choices: Hypothalamus → anterior pituitary ACTH → adrenal cortex → cortisol
Hypothalamus → posterior pituitary TSH → adrenal medulla → cortisol
Pancreas → insulin → adrenal cortex → cortisol
Thyroid → T4 → posterior pituitary → cortisol
authoredQuestions.answer: Hypothalamus → anterior pituitary ACTH → adrenal cortex → cortisol
authoredQuestions.cue: This is the slower HPA-style endocrine pathway.
authoredQuestions.explanation: ACTH is the tropic pituitary signal to the adrenal cortex.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which statement about cortisol is supported by the textbook?
choices: Cortisol has anti-inflammatory and immune-suppressing effects
Cortisol's main effect is to increase inflammation
Cortisol is released from the adrenal medulla
Cortisol is a pancreatic hormone
authoredQuestions.answer: Cortisol has anti-inflammatory and immune-suppressing effects
authoredQuestions.cue: This corrects a conflicting teacher-slide phrase.
authoredQuestions.explanation: The textbook explicitly describes cortisol as a natural anti-inflammatory.

authoredQuestions.prompt: How does aldosterone tend to increase blood volume and pressure?
choices: It increases kidney Na+ reabsorption, and water follows
It blocks all kidney sodium reabsorption
It increases glucose excretion
It destroys red blood cells
authoredQuestions.answer: It increases kidney Na+ reabsorption, and water follows
authoredQuestions.cue: Retained sodium changes osmotic water movement.
authoredQuestions.explanation: More Na+ retention promotes water retention and greater blood volume.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which pancreatic cells release insulin?
choices: Beta cells
Alpha cells
Adrenal cortical cells
Parathyroid cells
authoredQuestions.answer: Beta cells
authoredQuestions.explanation: Insulin release rises when blood glucose is high.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which pancreatic cells release glucagon?
choices: Alpha cells
Beta cells
Posterior-pituitary cells
Thyroid follicle cells
authoredQuestions.answer: Alpha cells
authoredQuestions.explanation: Glucagon release rises when blood glucose is low.

authoredQuestions.prompt: After a meal, which sequence best describes normal blood-glucose regulation?
choices: Glucose rises → insulin rises → uptake/storage increase → glucose falls
Glucose rises → glucagon rises → glycogen breakdown rises → glucose rises further
Glucose rises → ADH rises → kidney glucose uptake
Glucose rises → PTH rises → calcium release
authoredQuestions.answer: Glucose rises → insulin rises → uptake/storage increase → glucose falls
authoredQuestions.explanation: Insulin counteracts the post-meal rise in blood glucose.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Between meals, blood glucose falls. Which response is expected?
choices: Glucagon rises and promotes liver glucose release
Insulin rises and increases glycogen storage
Calcitonin rises and releases liver glycogen
ADH falls to raise glucose
authoredQuestions.answer: Glucagon rises and promotes liver glucose release
authoredQuestions.explanation: This complements insulin's glucose-lowering action.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes type 1 from type 2 diabetes mellitus?
choices: Type 1 commonly involves autoimmune beta-cell destruction; type 2 commonly begins with insulin resistance
Type 1 is an ADH disorder; type 2 is a thyroid disorder
Type 1 always results from diet; type 2 is always present at birth
Both are caused by excess insulin
authoredQuestions.answer: Type 1 commonly involves autoimmune beta-cell destruction; type 2 commonly begins with insulin resistance
authoredQuestions.explanation: Both affect glucose regulation but through different core mechanisms.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which pair is antagonistic in regulating the same variable?
choices: Insulin and glucagon
TSH and insulin
ADH and hGH
Cortisol and photopsin
authoredQuestions.answer: Insulin and glucagon
authoredQuestions.cue: One lowers and one raises blood glucose.
authoredQuestions.explanation: Their opposing effects stabilize blood glucose through negative feedback.

authoredQuestions.prompt: A hormone is produced in one brain region, transported down axons, and released from a second structure into blood. Which example fits?
choices: ADH: hypothalamus → posterior pituitary release
TSH: hypothalamus → posterior pituitary release
Insulin: hypothalamus → pancreas release
T4: pituitary → thyroid release
authoredQuestions.answer: ADH: hypothalamus → posterior pituitary release
authoredQuestions.cue: Produced and released are different locations here.
authoredQuestions.explanation: This is a core hypothalamus-posterior pituitary relationship.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which comparison of the two major stress pathways is correct?
choices: Adrenal medulla is activated rapidly by sympathetic neurons; adrenal cortex participates in a slower hormone cascade involving ACTH
Both branches require TSH
Both branches are triggered only by insulin
The adrenal cortex is the direct neural branch and medulla is the ACTH branch
authoredQuestions.answer: Adrenal medulla is activated rapidly by sympathetic neurons; adrenal cortex participates in a slower hormone cascade involving ACTH
authoredQuestions.explanation: The upstream control and time course differ.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Compare the anterior and posterior pituitary in terms of hormone production, control and release.
answerKey: Anterior pituitary synthesizes its own hormones
Anterior pituitary is regulated by hypothalamic releasing/inhibiting hormones through portal blood
Posterior pituitary stores/releases ADH and oxytocin made in hypothalamic neurons
Posterior relationship is neural/axonal
authoredQuestions.explanation: The key distinction is not merely front versus back; it is endocrine synthesis versus neural storage/release.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Trace the ADH response to dehydration from detection to kidney effect and feedback.
answerKey: Body fluids become concentrated/volume-pressure falls
Hypothalamic osmoreceptors/control detects change
ADH produced in hypothalamus and released from posterior pituitary
Kidney water reabsorption increases
Urine becomes lower-volume/more concentrated
Restoration reduces ADH drive
authoredQuestions.explanation: A complete answer must correctly distinguish synthesis and release locations.

authoredQuestions.prompt: A patient has low T4 because the thyroid cannot respond properly to TSH. Predict T4 and TSH levels and explain using negative feedback.
answerKey: T4 low
Reduced T4 feedback causes elevated hypothalamic/pituitary drive
TSH high if pituitary axis is intact
Thyroid still fails to produce adequate T4
authoredQuestions.explanation: This checks feedback reasoning rather than memorizing symptoms.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Compare the short-term adrenal-medulla stress response with the longer-term adrenal-cortex response.
answerKey: Medulla receives direct sympathetic neural stimulation
Medulla releases epinephrine/norepinephrine rapidly
Cortex receives endocrine stimulation including ACTH for cortisol
Cortisol has slower/longer metabolic effects and anti-inflammatory/immune-suppressing effects
Aldosterone influences Na+/water retention and blood pressure
authoredQuestions.explanation: Do not state that cortisol increases inflammation.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Explain how insulin and glucagon work as antagonistic hormones in a negative-feedback system.
answerKey: High glucose stimulates beta-cell insulin
Insulin promotes uptake/storage and lowers glucose
Low glucose stimulates alpha-cell glucagon
Glucagon promotes liver glucose release and raises glucose
Each response reduces the stimulus for its own release
authoredQuestions.explanation: The strongest answer traces both sides of the loop.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Correct this statement: 'The posterior pituitary makes ADH, ACTH causes the adrenal medulla to release epinephrine, and cortisol increases inflammation.'
answerKey: ADH is synthesized in hypothalamic neurons and released from posterior pituitary terminals
Adrenal medulla is stimulated rapidly by sympathetic neurons
ACTH acts mainly on adrenal cortex in the cortisol pathway
Cortisol is anti-inflammatory/immune-suppressing
authoredQuestions.explanation: This single item targets three high-value source/confusion points.

generatorGuidance.flashcards: Use hormone/gland, trigger, target, effect, and feedback relationships rather than term-only cards.
generatorGuidance.fillInBlanks: Blank one biologically meaningful element in a reviewed pathway. Accept abbreviations such as TSH, ACTH, ADH, hGH and PTH when unambiguous.
generatorGuidance.multipleChoice: Use authoredQuestions directly first. Additional items may be generated from the structured concept records only when exactly one option is defensible.
generatorGuidance.mixedPractice: Blend MC, hormone-matrix matching, pathway ordering, error correction, data/patient scenarios, and labeling from labeling-manifest.json.
generatorGuidance.review: Emphasize source → trigger → target → effect → feedback. Do not expose source quiz keys verbatim.
